titel: The witnesses of the nullity trial
autor: Depositions taken by the commissioners of the nullity trial, recorded in Latin by its notaries
quelle: J. Quicherat (ed.), Procès de condamnation et de réhabilitation de Jeanne d'Arc, dite la Pucelle, vol. II (Paris: Renouard, 1844), pp. 418–419, 436–437, and vol. III (1845), pp. 5–6, 86–87, 135–137, 156–157. Internet Archive, procsdecondam02joanuoft and procsdecondam03joanuoft. Public domain.
hinweis: Six depositions, excerpted and read against the page images. The record is in Latin; Jeanne's words, when a witness reports them, sometimes stand in French. Cuts are marked [...]. The English is this site's working translation (CC0); Murray's English (1902) was compared.

sections.blurb: From the inquiry in her own country: a childhood friend on the fairies' tree and her own tears when Jeanne left, and the squire who took her to the king on the conversation at Vaucouleurs.

units.orig: [...] per dictum suum juramentum dixit quod ipsa Johanna erat bona, simplex et dulcis filia, ac ibat libenter et sæpe ad ecclesiam et loca sacra, et sæpe habebat verecundiam eo quod gentes dicebant sibi quod nimis devote ibat ad ecclesiam ; audivit enim dici curato, tunc temporis exsistenti, quod pluries confitebatur. Occupabat se dicta Johanna sicut cæteræ puellæ faciunt ; necessaria domus faciebat ac nebat, et aliquando animalia sui patris, prout vidit, custodiebat. [...] dixit quod arbor illa vocatur l'abre Dominarum ab antiquo, et dicebatur antiquitus quod Dominæ quæ vocantur fées ibant ad illam arborem ; attamen nunquam audivit quod aliquis unquam aliquas viderit. Dixit etiam quod puellæ et pueri dictæ villæ consueverunt ire ad arborem et ad Fontem Rannorum, in die dominico Lætare Jherusalem, dicto des Fontaines, et secum portant panem ; et ipsa testis cum Johanna la Pucelle, quæ erat socia sua, fuit alias cum aliis juvenculis ad dictam arborem, in dicto dominico des Fontaines ; et ibidem comedebant, spatiabant et jocabant. [...] dixit quod nescivit recessum dictæ Johannetæ ; quæ testis propter hoc multum flevit, quia eam multum propter suam bonitatem diligebat, et quod sua socia erat. [...] dixit quod semper ipsa Johanna fuit in Novo-Castro cum patre et matre suis, quia ipsa testis in dicto Novo-Castro tunc temporis fuit, et illam semper vidit.
units.en: [...] on her oath she said that Jeanne was a good, simple and gentle girl, and went willingly and often to church and to holy places, and was often ashamed because people told her she went to church too devoutly; she heard the parish priest of that time say that she often went to confession. Jeanne busied herself as other girls do: she did the work of the house and spun, and sometimes, as the witness saw, she kept her father's beasts. [...] She said that the tree has been called the Ladies' Tree from of old, and that it was said in old times that ladies called fairies went to that tree; but she never heard that anyone had ever seen any. She said too that the girls and boys of the village used to go to the tree and to the spring of the Rannes on Laetare Sunday, called the Sunday of the Springs, and to take bread with them; and the witness went to the tree with Jeanne the Maid, who was her friend, and with other young girls on that Sunday of the Springs; and there they ate, walked about and played. [...] She said that she did not know of Jeanne's departure; and the witness wept much for it, because she loved her much for her goodness, and because she was her friend. [...] She said that Jeanne was always at Neufchâteau with her father and mother, for the witness was at Neufchâteau at that time and saw her all the time.
units.note: Hauviette, wife of Gérard of Sionne, about forty-five, examined at Domrémy on Friday 30 January 1456. She was three or four years younger than Jeanne. The questions put to the Domrémy witnesses followed the charges of 1431 point by point: her devotion, the fairies' tree (Art. Twelve [1]), her stay at Neufchâteau (compare Mon. [1]). The cuts are the clerk's formulas between the articles.

units.titel: Jean de Metz: 'even if I wear my feet down to the knees'
units.orig: [...] dum dicta Johanna la Pucelle perventa fuit ad locum et villam de Vallis-Colore, Tullensis diœcesis, ipse testis loquens vidit dictam Johannam indutam pauperibus vestibus, rubeis, muliebribus ; et erat locata in domo cujusdam Henrici Le Royer, dictæ villæ de Vallis-Colore ; qui locutus fuit sibi, dicendo : « Amica mea, quid hic facitis ? oportetne quod rex expellatur a regno, et quod simus Anglici ? » Quæ Puella tunc sibi respondit : « Ego veni huc ad cameram Regis, locutum Roberto de Baudricuria, ut me velit ducere aut duci facere ad Regem ; qui non curat de me neque de verbis meis ; attamen, antequam sit media quadragesima, oportet quod ego sim versus Regem, si ego deberem perdere pedes usque ad genua. Nullus enim in mundo, nec reges, nec duces, nec filia regis Scotiæ, aut alii, possunt recuperare regnum Franciæ, nec est ei succursus nisi de memet, quamvis ego mallem nere juxta meam pauperem matrem, quia non est status meus ; sed oportet ut ego vadam, et hoc faciam, quia Dominus meus vult ut ita faciam. » Et dum idem testis quæreret ab ea quis esset ejus Dominus, dicebat ipsa Puella quod erat Deus. Et tunc idem Johannes, testis, promisit eidem Puellæ, per fidem suam in sua manu tactam, quod eam, Deo duce, duceret versus Regem ; et tunc idem testis loquens petiit sibi quando vellet recedere ; quæ dicebat : « Citius nunc quam cras, et cras quam post. » Et petiit sibi idem testis iterato si cum suis vestibus vellet ire ; quæ respondit quod libenter haberet vestes hominis. Et tunc idem testis de famulis suis tradidit sibi vestes et calceamenta, ad induendum [...].
units.en: [...] when Jeanne the Maid came to the town of Vaucouleurs, in the diocese of Toul, the witness saw her dressed in poor red clothes, a woman's; she was lodged in the house of one Henri Le Royer of Vaucouleurs. He spoke to her, saying: 'My friend, what are you doing here? Must the king be driven from the kingdom, and must we be English?' The Maid answered him: 'I have come here to a royal town, to speak to Robert de Baudricourt, that he may take me or have me taken to the king; but he cares nothing for me or for my words. And yet before mid-Lent I must be with the king, even if I have to wear my feet down to the knees. For no one in the world, neither kings nor dukes nor the king of Scotland's daughter nor any other, can recover the kingdom of France, and there is no help for it but from me; though I would rather spin beside my poor mother, for this is not my condition; but I must go and do it, because my Lord wills that I should do so.' And when the witness asked her who her Lord was, the Maid said it was God. Then Jean, the witness, promised the Maid, with his faith given in her hand, that, God leading, he would take her to the king; and he asked her when she wished to leave. She said: 'Sooner now than tomorrow, and tomorrow than after.' And he asked her again whether she wanted to go in her own clothes; she answered that she would gladly have a man's clothes. Then the witness gave her clothes and shoes of one of his servants to put on [...].
units.note: Jean de Nouillompont, called de Metz, about fifty-seven, examined at Vaucouleurs on Saturday 31 January 1456. 'Ad cameram Regis': Quicherat's footnote gives the French, 'je suis venue cy à chambre de roy', a town held directly of the crown. The king of Scotland's daughter was Margaret, then promised to the dauphin. The cut goes on: the people of Vaucouleurs had a man's clothes made for her and bought her a horse for about sixteen francs, and he and Bertrand de Poulengy took her to Chinon about the first Sunday of Lent 1429. The man's clothes, which the court of 1431 treated as a sin and the occasion of her relapse (Ouen Relapse [2]), were here given to her for the road by a squire of Vaucouleurs.

sections.titel: The year of the Maid, remembered (1456)
sections.blurb: Dunois on her first words to him at Orléans and the wind that turned, and the widow who shared her house and bed at Bourges on the rosaries the women brought.

units.titel: Dunois: 'En nom Dieu' and the wind on the Loire
units.orig: [...] et quia exercitus regis, seu armatorum hujusmodi victualia conducentium, non videbatur dicto domino deponenti et aliis dominis capitaneis sufficiens ad resistendum, et conducendum ipsa victualia infra civitatem, imo maxime, quia opus erat habere naves seu bastellos, quas seu quos cum difficultate habere poterant, pro eundo quæsitum dicta victualia, quia oportebat ascendere contra cursum aquæ, et ventus erat totaliter contrarius, tunc ipsa Johanna dixit verba quæ sequuntur : « Estis vos Bastardus Aurelianensis ? » Qui respondit : « Ita sum, et lætor de adventu vestro. » Tunc ipsa dixit eidem domino deponenti : « Estis vos qui dedistis consilium quod venerim huc, de isto latere ripariæ, et quod non iverim de directo ubi erat Tallebot et Anglici ? » Qui deponens respondit quod ipse et alii sapientiores eo dederant illud consilium, credentes melius facere et securius. Tunc ipsa Johanna dixit in isto modo : « En nom Dieu, consilium Dei Domini nostri est securius et sapientius quam vestrum. Vos credidistis me decipere, et vosmet ipsum plus decipitis, quia ego adduco vobis meliorem succursum quam venerit unquam cuicumque militi aut civitati, quia est succursus a Rege cœlorum. Non tamen procedit amore mei, sed ab ipso Deo, qui, ad requestam sancti Ludovici et sancti Karoli Magni, habuit pietatem de villa Aurelianensi, nec voluit pati quod inimici haberent corpus domini Aurelianensis et villam ejus. » Dicitque præterea dictus deponens quod statim, et quasi in momento, ventus, qui erat contrarius et valde impediens ne ascenderent naves in quibus erant victualia ad civitatem Aurelianensem, mutatus est et factus ei propitius ; quare statim tensa sunt vela, et dictus deponens intravit bastellos seu naves, et cum eo frater Nicolaus de Geresme, nunc magnus prior Franciæ ; et transiverunt ultra ecclesiam Sancti Lupi, invitis Anglicis. Extunc dictus deponens habuit bonam spem de ea et plus quam ante [...].
units.en: [...] And because the king's army, the men-at-arms bringing the supplies, did not seem to the witness and the other captains strong enough to resist and bring the supplies into the city; and above all because boats were needed, which could be had only with difficulty, to go and fetch the supplies, since they had to go up against the current, and the wind was wholly contrary; then Jeanne spoke these words: 'Are you the Bastard of Orléans?' He answered: 'I am, and I am glad of your coming.' Then she said to the witness: 'Was it you who gave the advice that I should come here, on this side of the river, and not go straight to where Talbot and the English were?' The witness answered that he and others wiser than he had given that advice, thinking it better and safer. Then Jeanne said: 'En nom Dieu, the counsel of God our Lord is safer and wiser than yours. You thought to deceive me, and you deceive yourself more, for I bring you better help than ever came to any knight or any city, for it is help from the King of Heaven. Yet it does not come for love of me, but from God himself, who, at the request of Saint Louis and Saint Charlemagne, has had pity on the town of Orléans, and would not suffer the enemy to have the body of the lord of Orléans and his town.' And the witness says further that at once, almost in a moment, the wind, which had been contrary and had kept the boats carrying the supplies from going up to the city, changed and became favourable; the sails were spread at once, and the witness got into the boats, and with him brother Nicole de Giresme, now grand prior of France, and they passed beyond the church of Saint-Loup in spite of the English. From then on the witness had good hope of her, more than before [...].
units.note: Jean, count of Dunois, the Bastard of Orléans, examined at Orléans in the inquiry of 1456. The 'body of the lord of Orléans' is his half-brother, Duke Charles of Orléans, a prisoner in England since Agincourt (1415). The scene is 29 April 1429, the day of her entry (Orl. Arrival [2]). 'En nom Dieu' stands in French in the Latin record, as it gives the companion game its name. Nicole de Giresme is the knight of Rhodes who first crossed the broken arch at the Tourelles (Orl. Tourelles [2]).

units.orig: Dicit insuper quod [quum] aliquando fabularentur ad invicem, et eidem Johannæ diceretur quod ipsa non dubitabat ire ad insultus, quia ipsa bene sciebat quod non cæderetur : ipsa respondebat quod non habebat aliquam securitatem amplius quam cæteri armati. Et narrabat aliquando ipsa Johanna qualiter fuerat examinata per clericos, et quod eis responderat : « Il y a ès livres de nostre Seigneur plus que ès vostres. » [...] Dicit etiam quod ipsa Johanna erat multum simplex et ignorans, et nihil penitus sciebat, videre loquentis, nisi in facto guerræ. Et recordatur ipsa loquens quod plures mulieres veniebant ad domum loquentis, dum ipsa Johanna in eadem morabatur, et apportabant paternostres et alia signacula, ut ipsa tangeret ea ; de quo ipsa Johanna ridebat, eidem loquenti dicendo : « Tangatis vosmet, quia ita bona erunt ex tactu vestro sicut ex meo. »
units.en: She says moreover that once, when they were talking together and it was said to Jeanne that she was not afraid to go into assaults because she knew well she would not be killed, she answered that she had no more assurance than the other men-at-arms. And Jeanne sometimes told how she had been examined by the clerks, and that she had answered them: 'There is more in Our Lord's books than in yours.' [...] She says also that Jeanne was very simple and ignorant, and knew nothing at all, in the witness's view, except in the matter of war. And the witness remembers that many women came to her house while Jeanne was staying there, and brought rosaries and other tokens for her to touch; at which Jeanne laughed, saying to the witness: 'Touch them yourselves, for they will be as good from your touch as from mine.'
units.note: Marguerite La Touroulde, widow of René de Bouligny, a councillor of the king, about sixty-four, examined in Paris in 1456. Jeanne lodged with her at Bourges for three weeks after the coronation, in the autumn of 1429, and the two shared a bed most nights. The cut tells of the duke of Lorraine, whom Jeanne told to take back his good wife, and of her hatred of dice.

sections.titel: The men of the first trial (Rouen, May 1456)
sections.blurb: The notary on the English secretaries who wrote down what they liked and on the bishop's 'fine trial', and the usher on the schedule of eight lines she signed at Saint-Ouen.

units.orig: [...] Interrogatus ipse testis, et ostenso sibi processu facto in gallico, in quo sunt in capite quorumdam articulorum plura Nota, quid deserviunt illa Nota : respondit quod in primis interrogationibus factis Johannæ fuit factus maximus tumultus, in prima die suæ interrogationis, in cappella castri Rothomagensis, et interrumpebantur quasi singula verba ipsius Johannæ, dum loqueretur de suis apparitionibus, quia ibidem erant aliqui secretarii regis Angliæ, duo aut tres, qui registrabant prout volebant dicta et depositiones ejusdem Johannæ, omittentes excusationes ejusdem, et ea quæ faciebant ad sui deonerationem. Et ipse loquens tunc de hoc conquestus est, dicens quod, nisi apponeretur alius ordo, quod ipse non susciperet onus scribendi in ipsa materia ; et ob hoc in crastinum fuit mutatus locus, et convenerunt in quadam aula castri exsistente prope magnam aulam ; et erant duo Anglici custodientes ostium. Et quoniam aliquando erat difficultas super responsionibus ipsius Johannæ et dictis, et quod aliqui dicebant quod ita non responderat sicut erat scriptum per loquentem, ubi ipsi videbatur difficultas, ponebat Nota in capite, ut iterum interrogaretur et cessaret difficultas. Et hoc est quod denotant illa Nota in capite posita. [...] Et ipse loquens, in hac materia fuit compulsus ut interesset sicut notarius, et hoc invitus fecit, quia non fuisset ausus contradicere præcepto dominorum de Consilio regis. Et prosequebantur Anglici hujusmodi processum, et expensis suis fuit deductus. Credit tamen episcopum Belvacensem non fuisse pressum ad deducendum processum contra dictam Johannam, nec etiam promotorem ; imo voluntarie hoc egerunt. De assessoribus et aliis consiliariis, credit quod non fuissent ausi contradicere venire, nec erat aliquis qui non timeret ; nam in principio processus fuit facta quædam congregatio, in qua erant dominus episcopus Belvacensis, abbas Fiscampnensis, magister Nicolaus Loyseleur, et plures alii, in quadam domo prope castrum, qui mandarunt pro loquente ; ac eidem loquenti dixit episcopus quod oportebat quod serviret regi, et quod intendebant facere unum pulchrum processum contra dictam Johannam, quodque advisaret unum alium notarium, qui secum assisteret ; et tunc nominavit Boisguillaume.
units.en: [...] Questioned, and shown the trial record made in French, in which there is a 'Nota' at the head of several articles, as to what those 'Nota' are for, he answered that at the first interrogations of Jeanne, on the first day of her questioning, in the chapel of the castle of Rouen, there was a very great tumult, and almost every word of Jeanne's was interrupted while she spoke of her apparitions, because there were some secretaries of the king of England there, two or three, who recorded her words and statements as they pleased, leaving out her excuses and whatever served to clear her. And the witness complained of it then, saying that unless another order were put in place he would not take on the charge of writing in this matter; and for this reason the place was changed the next day, and they met in a hall of the castle near the great hall, with two Englishmen guarding the door. And because there was sometimes difficulty about Jeanne's answers and words, and some said she had not answered as the witness had written, where the difficulty seemed to him to lie he put 'Nota' at the head, so that she should be questioned again and the difficulty settled. That is what those 'Nota' at the head mean. [...] And the witness was compelled to take part in this matter as notary, and did it unwillingly, because he would not have dared to oppose the order of the lords of the king's council. And the English pursued this trial, and it was conducted at their expense. He believes, however, that the bishop of Beauvais was not pressed into conducting the trial against Jeanne, nor the promoter either; rather they did it willingly. Of the assessors and other counsellors, he believes that they would not have dared refuse to come, and there was no one who was not afraid; for at the beginning of the trial there was a gathering, at which were the bishop of Beauvais, the abbot of Fécamp, master Nicolas Loiseleur and several others, in a house near the castle, who sent for the witness; and the bishop told him that he must serve the king, and that they intended to make a fine trial against Jeanne, and that he should find another notary to assist him; and then he named Boisguillaume.
units.note: Guillaume Manchon, priest, about sixty, chief notary of the trial of 1431, examined at Rouen on Wednesday 12 May 1456. It was his French minute that survived (Interr. Prison [1]–[4]); he testified that the Latin record was made from it 'long after her death' by himself and Thomas de Courcelles. His evidence cuts both ways: the record he kept is the best witness against the court, and he signed it. Between the cuts he says she asked to hear Mass on Palm Sunday and at Easter and was allowed to confess only to Loiseleur; just after, that she asked again and again to be put in the Church's prison and was refused, because, he believes, the English would not have handed her over.

units.titel: Massieu: 'about eight lines, and no more'
units.orig: [...] quantum ad abjurationem de qua in articulis fit mentio, quod quando fuit facta prædicatio per magistrum Nicolaum Erardi in Sancto Audoeno, quod ipse Erardi tenebat quamdam schedulam abjurationis, et dixit Johannæ : « Tu adjurabis et signabis istam schedulam. » Et tunc illa schedula fuit loquenti tradita ad legendum, et eam legit loquens coram eadem Johanna. Et est bene memor quod in eadem schedula cavebatur quod de cætero non portaret arma, habitum virilem, capillos rasos, et multa alia de quibus non recordatur. Et bene scit quod illa schedula continebat circiter octo lineas, et non amplius ; et scit firmiter quod non erat illa de qua in processu fit mentio, quia aliam ab illa quæ est inserta in processu legit ipse loquens, et signavit ipsa Johanna. Ulterius dicit quod, dum ipsa Johanna requireretur de signando dictam schedulam, ortum fuit magnum murmur inter præsentes, adeo quod audivit quod episcopus dixit cuidam : « Vos emendabitis mihi, » asserens sibi fuisse illatam injuriam, et quod non procederet ultra quousque sibi fuisset facta emenda. Et interim ipse loquens advertebat eamdem Johannam de periculo sibi imminente, super signatura dictæ schedulæ ; et bene videbat loquens quod ipsa Johanna non intelligebat dictam schedulam, nec periculum quod sibi imminebat. Et tunc ipsa Johanna, oppressa ut signaret dictam schedulam, respondit : « Videatur ipsa schedula per clericos et Ecclesiam, in quorum manibus debeo poni ; et si mihi consilium dederint quod habeam eam signare, et agere quæ mihi dicuntur, ego libenter faciam. » Tunc ipse magister Guillelmus Erardi dixit : « Facias nunc, alioquin tu per ignem finies dies tuos hodie. » Et tunc ipsa Johanna respondit quod malebat signare quam cremari [...].
units.en: [...] as to the abjuration mentioned in the articles: when the sermon was preached by master Nicolas [sic] Érard at Saint-Ouen, Érard held a schedule of abjuration and said to Jeanne: 'You will abjure [adjurabis, as printed] and sign this schedule.' Then the schedule was handed to the witness to read, and he read it before Jeanne. And he remembers well that it provided that she should not in future bear arms, wear men's clothes, or have her hair cut short, and many other things he does not remember. And he knows well that the schedule contained about eight lines, and no more; and he knows firmly that it was not the one mentioned in the trial record, because the one he read, and Jeanne signed, was another than the one inserted in the record. He says further that while Jeanne was being asked to sign the schedule, a great murmur arose among those present, so much that he heard the bishop say to someone, 'You will make amends to me,' declaring that an injury had been done him and that he would not proceed further until amends had been made. Meanwhile the witness warned Jeanne of the danger that threatened her over the signing of the schedule; and he saw well that she did not understand the schedule, nor the danger she was in. And then Jeanne, pressed to sign, answered: 'Let the schedule be seen by the clerks and the Church, into whose hands I ought to be put; and if they advise me to sign it and do what I am told, I will do it willingly.' Then master Guillaume Érard said: 'Do it now, or else you will end your days by fire today.' And then Jeanne answered that she would rather sign than be burned [...].
units.note: Jean Massieu, priest, the court's usher, who led her to and from the sessions, examined at Rouen in May 1456. Quicherat prints 'Nicolaum Erardi' at the start and 'Guillelmus Erardi' below; the preacher was Guillaume Érard. The schedule entered in the record (Ouen Abjuration [2]) fills the better part of two pages in Quicherat's print. Massieu's 'about eight lines' was the nullity court's main evidence that she had signed something other than what was entered against her. The cut goes on: there was a great tumult among the people and many stones were thrown; when she asked the promoter whether she would not now be put in the hands of the Church, and where she was to go, he answered: to the castle of Rouen; and she was taken there in women's clothes.
